summary: Customers could delete shared ticket drafts prepared by agents
description:
Shared drafts prepared by agents could be deleted by customers who were not allowed to use them. A customer could remove the shared new-ticket drafts of any group while creating a ticket, and the shared reply drafts of tickets they could access as a customer while replying to them. Agents without access to a group could not delete its drafts. Shared drafts are enabled per group by default, and no hard-to-obtain information was needed.

The content of the drafts was not disclosed, and no other ticket data could be read or changed. The effect was limited to the loss of draft text that agents had prepared.

summary: Partial administrators could delete records and read restricted data via core workflow conditions
description:
Administrators with only the permission to manage core workflows could configure a workflow condition that made the server call internal functions on the record being evaluated, instead of only reading its fields. The condition ran whenever the workflow was evaluated, which happens when any user, including customers, opens, changes or saves a form it applies to.

This could have been used to delete tickets, users or other records, actions reserved for other administrative permissions, and to read data the administrator was not allowed to see, such as fields hidden from them and other users' API tokens, including those of full administrators.

Exploitation required an authenticated account with the core workflow administration permission. Installations where only fully trusted users hold this permission were not exposed.

cwes.name: Use of Externally-Controlled Input to Select Classes or Code

summary: Delegated administrators could read stored records and credentials through template placeholders
description:
Users who were permitted to manage only certain configuration areas, without full administrator permissions, could have read data outside their permissions through the placeholders Zammad supports in configurable texts. This included protected system settings such as the application secret, any stored record, and the credentials of configured email accounts. The values could have been made visible in content the user could read, for example an internal ticket note created by a trigger, an inserted text module or a rendered object attribute link.

The attack required an account with the permission to manage triggers, schedulers, macros, text modules, object attributes, AI agents, AI text tools or email channels. Installations that grant these permissions only to full administrators were not affected.

cwes.name: Use of Externally-Controlled Input to Select Classes or Code
Improper Neutralization of Special Elements Used in a Template Engine

summary: Customer ticket search matches content of internal articles
description:
Ticket search for customers did not exclude data that is visible to agents only. While customers could only find their own tickets and tickets of organizations they share, the search term was also compared against internal articles, their attachments and other agent-only ticket information.

An authenticated customer could therefore find out whether such internal content on their own or their organization's tickets contained a chosen term, for example a name or an amount, by observing which tickets were returned. The content itself was never displayed. Installations using Elasticsearch were affected to a larger extent, as more agent-only ticket information was included in the search there.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Agent sessions disclosed macros and AI text tools of all groups
description:
Macros and AI text tools could be restricted to specific groups or deactivated. Every agent nevertheless received all macros and AI text tools of the system, including those of groups they had no access to and deactivated ones, with their full configuration: the actions of a macro, which can contain internal note texts and notification email recipients, subjects and bodies, and the prompt of an AI text tool. Deactivated ticket templates and the names of shared drafts in other groups were exposed the same way.

Any agent account was sufficient. The exposure was read-only: the records could not be changed, and macros of other groups still could not be applied.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Administrators could replace internal components of system settings, incl. password authentication
description:
### Impact

Several system settings store the name of an internal server component that Zammad loads and runs, for example the backends for password authentication, ticket numbering, dashboard statistics and external services. The server did not check that a saved value named a component intended for that setting.

An administrator with the permission for one of these settings could have chosen a different component. For the password authentication settings, this could have made Zammad accept any password for every account without two-factor authentication configured, including administrator accounts. This change was not visible in the admin interface and stayed in effect after the permission was revoked. For the other settings, the affected feature could have been made to fail.

Exploitation required an authenticated account with an administrative permission for one of these settings. Installations where only fully trusted users hold administrative permissions were not exposed to other users.

cwes.name: Use of Externally-Controlled Input to Select Classes or Code

summary: Partial administrators could run unintended server components via core workflows
description:
Administrators with only the permission to manage core workflows could configure a workflow so that the server ran internal code components that are not meant to be used in core workflows. These components ran whenever the workflow was evaluated, which happens when any user, including customers, opens or changes a form it applies to.

This could have been used to perform actions reserved for other administrative permissions, such as resetting the notification settings of all agents, and to tie up server resources on every form load, slowing down or breaking forms for other users.

Exploitation required an authenticated account with the core workflow administration permission. Installations where only fully trusted users hold this permission were not exposed.

cwes.name: Use of Externally-Controlled Input to Select Classes or Code

summary: Memory corruption in Ruby's regular expression compiler via administrator-configured patterns
description:
Zammad shipped with a Ruby version whose regular expression engine (Onigmo) could corrupt memory while compiling specially crafted patterns. The Ruby project fixed these flaws in Ruby 3.4.12; GitLab reported them as CVE-2026-89078, CVE-2026-93577, CVE-2026-97229 and CVE-2026-110264.

Zammad compiles regular expressions that are configured in Core Workflows, postmaster filters, the monitoring integrations, the CTI integration, the chat channel and some email settings. A user with the matching administrator permission could have entered a crafted pattern that corrupted the memory of the Zammad process. Depending on the pattern, this could have crashed the process or, in the worst case, allowed code execution on the server with the privileges of the Zammad service account. Agents, customers and unauthenticated users could not supply such patterns.

Zammad now uses Ruby 3.4.12. Installations from source must update their Ruby version to 3.4.12 manually. The DEB and RPM packages and the official container images include the updated Ruby version.

summary: AI-generated knowledge base drafts could be saved into categories the agent was not allowed to edit
description:
When AI assistance generated a knowledge base answer draft from a ticket, the category it was filed under was not checked against the acting agent's permissions. An agent with editor permission on at least one category could therefore end up with a new draft in a category they were only allowed to read, or could not access at all. Creating the same answer manually was correctly refused. Existing answers could not be changed this way.

The drafts were unpublished and tagged as AI-generated, so nothing became publicly visible on its own.

Only installations with an AI provider configured, knowledge base draft generation enabled and per-category editor permissions were affected.

summary: Partial administrators could add unchecked options to system settings
description:
Administrators with a partial administrative permission, for example only the permission for security settings, could store additional internal options on the system settings they were allowed to change. The server acted on these options.

This could have been used to hide a setting from all administrators, including full administrators, so that it could no longer be viewed or changed through the user interface or API, and to make the server run internal code components chosen by the attacker whenever the setting was saved.

Exploitation required an authenticated account with at least one administrative permission that grants access to a system setting. Installations where only fully trusted users hold administrative permissions were not exposed to other users.

cwes.name: Use of Externally-Controlled Input to Select Classes or Code
Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes

summary: Denial of Service via Unauthenticated Websocket Message
description:
Zammad's websocket server could be terminated by a single message from an unauthenticated client. Incoming messages were accepted and processed before any authentication took place, and a message that did not have the expected structure was not rejected but ended the process instead.

While the service was down, real-time updates in the classic agent interface stopped and the Zammad Chat widget on public websites was unavailable. Ticket handling over HTTP continued to work, and no data could be read or changed. The service restarted automatically in most deployments, but the message could be repeated at will, and on systemd installations the default restart limit could leave the service stopped until an administrator intervened.

summary: Partial administrators could replace the product logo
description:
An authenticated user with permission to change at least one system setting, but without the branding permission, could have replaced the product logo of the Zammad system. The authorization check of the logo upload was performed against a setting chosen by the caller instead of the logo setting itself.

The replaced logo was shown to all users, including customers on the login page, and could have been used to make the system look defaced or to support phishing attempts. No data was disclosed and no other setting could be changed this way. Installations in which only full administrators hold any admin permission were not affected.

summary: Live updates of macros and AI text tools disclosed their identifiers and group assignments to all logged-in users
description:
Zammad sent live updates about macros and AI text tools to every logged-in user, regardless of their permissions. Whenever one of these records was created, changed or deleted, all open sessions received its internal identifier and the identifiers of the groups it was assigned to. Customers were included, although macros and AI text tools are not available to them at all.

Receiving this data required nothing beyond a logged-in account; the identifiers arrived on their own as soon as someone changed such a record.

The disclosure was limited to identifiers and group assignments. The name of a macro, the actions it performs, the instructions behind an AI text tool and any ticket or customer data were not included, and nothing could be changed. Installations in which only agents and administrators hold accounts were not affected.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Cross-site request forgery in realtime update endpoint
description:
One of the endpoints used for realtime updates in the web interface was not protected against cross-site request forgery. A third-party website visited by a logged-in Zammad user could have caused that user's browser to trigger realtime actions in the user's name, without the user's knowledge.

The impact depended on the permissions of the affected user. For users with permission to manage maintenance, it could have sent maintenance messages or a forced page reload to all connected users, for example to show a misleading message. For other users, it could have disrupted their own open sessions or changed their chat availability. No data was disclosed to the attacker.

summary: API token permission restrictions not applied to live update pushes
description:
Personal access tokens can be limited to a subset of their owner's permissions. Zammad did not apply this limit to the live updates it pushed through one of its browser connection channels. Anyone holding a restricted token could have used it to receive the owner's ticket overview lists and activity stream, including ticket metadata and the names and contact details of the users and organizations involved, even if the token itself had no ticket permissions.

Exploitation required possession of a valid token of an agent or customer account. Access was read-only and limited to data the token owner could see in their overviews and activity stream; ticket article content was not exposed. Installations where API token access is disabled were not affected.

summary: Missing limit on failed two-factor attempts allows brute-forcing the second factor
description:
Failed two-factor authentication attempts at login were neither counted towards the account lockout nor rate limited, and users were not notified about them. An attacker who already knew a user's password could therefore keep guessing the one-time code of the authenticator app method without ever being locked out.

A successful guess required sustained effort over days per account, but several accounts could be targeted in parallel. It gave full access to the affected account with that user's permissions, including all tickets and customer data the user could see.

Only accounts using the authenticator app method were affected. Security keys and recovery codes could not be guessed this way.

cwes.name: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts

summary: Public knowledge base feed disclosed titles of non-public categories
description:
The public knowledge base feed of a category did not check whether the category was meant to be visible on the public help center. An unauthenticated visitor could have read the titles of categories that contained only internal or draft answers, and therefore stay hidden on the public help center. Because category identifiers are sequential, all such titles could have been collected, and the responses also revealed which categories existed.

The contents of internal or draft answers were not exposed; the feed only ever listed published answers. No data could be modified.

Only installations with an active knowledge base were affected, and only if it contained categories without published answers. How sensitive this is depends on what the category titles of such a knowledge base reveal.

summary: Knowledge base search showed answers from restricted categories to editors
description:
When knowledge base categories were restricted per role, users who could edit the knowledge base could still find answers and categories in the knowledge base search that their role had no access to. This also happened during a normal search on the public help site while logged in.

The results included answer titles, short excerpts or matching fragments of the answer content, tags and category titles, also for draft, internal and archived answers. The full answer could not be opened.

Only installations that use per-category knowledge base permissions to restrict users who can edit the knowledge base were affected. Read-only users and customers were not affected. This was a second path to the weakness described in GHSA-4m54-p3mr-22g2, which the earlier fix did not cover.

summary: Disclosure of inaccessible tickets via checklist references
description:
When an agent opened a ticket in the legacy user interface, Zammad also loaded checklists of other tickets that referenced it. If such a checklist belonged to a ticket in a group the agent had no access to, the server still included that ticket in its response, although the user interface did not display it.

This could have allowed an authenticated agent to read the attributes of tickets outside their groups, such as title, note and state, together with details of the related customer, owner and organization, and the checklist items of that ticket. Only tickets whose checklist referenced a ticket the agent could access were exposed. The agent could not choose which tickets to read, and no data could be modified.

summary: GitLab API token stored in clear text in the HTTP log
description:
Requests of the GitLab integration were recorded in the HTTP log with the GitLab API token in clear text, because the masking of sensitive values did not cover the way this integration sends its token.

Users with permission to view the integration logs (`admin.integration`) could therefore read the stored GitLab API token, although the integration settings hide it from them. With the token, they could access the connected GitLab instance within the token's scopes.

Only installations with the GitLab integration enabled were affected. Log entries written before the update may still contain the token, so administrators should rotate the GitLab API token after upgrading.

cwes.name: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File

summary: Revoked and refreshed OAuth2 tokens remained usable
description:
Zammad did not honor the revocation of OAuth2 tokens issued by its OAuth2 provider. An access token that was revoked by its client, or replaced by refreshing it, continued to be accepted for API requests until its regular expiry, by default up to two hours. A refresh token that had already been used to obtain a new access token was never revoked and could be used again to obtain further access tokens, without any time limit.

Anyone in possession of such a token, for example after it had leaked, could therefore keep reading and changing all data with the permissions of the user the token was issued for, in the case of a refresh token even after the client had already refreshed it. Installations that do not use OAuth2 applications were not affected.

summary: Channel type restriction bypass for partial channel administrators
description:
Users holding only the permission to manage SMS, Facebook or e-mail channels could have accessed channels of other types, such as e-mail, Microsoft 365, Google, Telegram or WhatsApp channels. The affected endpoints checked the general channel permission, but not whether the requested channel belonged to the channel type the user was allowed to manage.

With the SMS or Facebook channel permission, other channels could have been read, changed, disabled or deleted, while their passwords and access tokens remained masked. With the e-mail channel permission, the stored access token of a Microsoft 365 or Google channel could have been disclosed to the user.

This required an account with one of these partial admin permissions. Installations that grant these permissions only to full administrators were not affected.

summary: Maintenance mode was not enforced on real-time connections
description:
While maintenance mode was active, Zammad denied access to all users without the maintenance permission. The real-time connections that the browser uses did not apply that check consistently, and a user's session stayed valid after their requests had been refused. Logging such a user out was left to their client; where that did not happen, the user could have continued to read and change data over these connections for as long as maintenance mode stayed active.

The user kept only their regular permissions: they could not access any ticket, customer or setting beyond what their role and group access already allowed. Installations were only affected while maintenance mode was enabled.

summary: Agents could remove links to objects they had no access to
description:
Removing a link between two objects only checked the permissions of the requesting agent on one of the linked objects. An agent who was allowed to change a ticket could therefore remove links between that ticket and tickets or knowledge base answers they had no access to, for example tickets in groups they were not a member of. The legacy interface and the GraphQL API were both affected.

No content of the inaccessible object was disclosed, and the agent could not change anything else on it. The impact is limited to the integrity of links: relationships maintained by other teams could be removed without their knowledge. Customers could not exploit this.

summary: Account takeover via client-controlled identity in SSO authentication
description:
In installations with SSO authentication enabled, Zammad accepted the user identity from more than one source, and a source that the client could control took precedence over the identity set by the authenticating reverse proxy. The reverse proxy configurations shipped with Zammad and the documented SSO setup did not remove this client-controlled value.

This could have allowed a user who was able to reach the SSO endpoint through the proxy, for example any user authenticated against the directory service, to log in as any other Zammad user, including administrators, and to read and modify all data accessible to that user.

Only installations with SSO authentication enabled were affected. Restricting SSO to trusted proxy IP addresses did not prevent this. Administrators who cannot update immediately should make sure their reverse proxy removes the `Remote-User` request header from incoming client requests.

summary: Remote content and API path bypass via inline styles in HTML sanitizer
description:
The HTML sanitizer did not check the value of a background style that is allowed on some text and table elements. A specially crafted email or article could therefore have made the browser of an agent opening it load content from a foreign server, although loading of external content was blocked and no notice about blocked content was shown. The sender could have learned the agent's IP address, browser and time of reading.

The same weakness could have caused the agent's browser to request certain Zammad API endpoints in the agent's own session, for example ending that session.

No Zammad account was required; sending an email to a monitored address was enough.

summary: Remote image tracking and API path bypass via backslash URLs in HTML sanitizer
description:
The HTML sanitizer did not recognize certain malformed image URLs as pointing to an external host. An unauthenticated attacker who could send an email to a Zammad instance could have embedded images that were loaded when an agent viewed the article, even though external content is blocked. This revealed the agent's IP address, browser user agent and the time the article was read, and no notice about blocked content was shown.

The same weakness could have been used to make the agent's browser request Zammad API endpoints that change state via GET, for example signing the agent out when viewing the article. No ticket data was exposed and no other data could be altered.

summary: Session identifier still disclosed through GraphQL session and login responses
description:
The fix for GHSA-23hj-h8w6-rgm3 was incomplete. Zammad's GraphQL API, which serves the new desktop and mobile interfaces, still returned the signed-in user's session identifier in its session and login responses. Scripts running in that user's browser were therefore still able to read it, which the session cookie's `HttpOnly` flag is meant to prevent.

An attacker who had already gained script execution in a user's session, through a separate weakness, could copy the identifier to a machine of their own and act as that user from there for the life of the session, without their password or second factor. This included reading everything the account could see and creating or changing data in the user's name. The reach scaled with the privileges of the affected account.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Partial admin permissions allowed changing restricted system settings and account takeover
description:
Users with any partial administrative permission, for example only the permission to manage text modules, could read and change system settings that were meant for full administrators only. This included the developer mode, which allowed logging in to any account with a shared password, as well as the search index connection settings and their credentials.

As a result, such a user could have taken over any account without two-factor authentication configured, including full administrator accounts, and could have redirected indexed ticket data to a server of their choosing.

Installations that do not grant partial administrative permissions to any role or API token were not affected.

summary: Unauthenticated memory exhaustion via crafted image attachments
description:
Zammad generated preview images for incoming JPEG and PNG attachments without limiting the size of the decoded image. A small, specially crafted image file could therefore cause the processing Zammad process to allocate several gigabytes of memory and spend seconds of CPU time per attachment.

No authentication was required: an image attached to an email sent to any address monitored by a Zammad email channel was sufficient. Uploads by logged-in users were affected in the same way. Repeated attempts could exhaust the memory of the server, slowing down or interrupting the processing of emails and web requests. The impact depended on the memory available to the installation. No data could be read or modified.

cwes.name: Improper Handling of Highly Compressed Data (Data Amplification)
Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

summary: Delegated text module and trigger managers could read protected system settings
description:
Users who were permitted to manage only text modules or triggers, without full administrator permissions, could have read protected system settings that are reserved for administrators. These included the application secret and credentials stored in the system configuration, such as the Elasticsearch and proxy passwords and the client secrets of configured third-party login providers. The values could have been made visible in content that the user could read, for example an inserted text module or an internal ticket note created by a trigger.

The attack required an account with the text module (together with agent access) or the trigger administration permission. Installations that grant these permissions only to full administrators were not affected.

summary: Disclosure of internal service responses via external authentication profile images
description:
When a user logged in through an external authentication provider, Zammad fetched the profile image URL supplied by the provider and stored the response as the user's avatar without checking that it actually was an image. This fetch could also reach services on the internal network and on the Zammad host itself.

A user who could set their own profile image URL at a connected identity provider could have used this to read responses from internal services that do not require authentication, for example a local Elasticsearch instance holding ticket data.

Installations were only affected if they used an external authentication provider that lets users or third parties control the profile image URL. Providers that host profile images themselves were not affected.

summary: Organization list disclosure to customers without organization
description:
A customer user who was not assigned to any organization could have retrieved a list of all organizations in the system via the organization search and autocomplete functions. The list included the names, IDs and active state of organizations the customer had no access to, and in some views also their number of members.

The issue only affected customer accounts without any organization assignment; customers belonging to at least one organization were correctly limited to their own organizations. No ticket content, user details or other organization attributes were exposed, and no data could be modified.

summary: Customers kept receiving live updates of shared-organization tickets after leaving the organization
description:
Real-time GraphQL subscriptions kept using the authorization state a user had when their browser connection was opened. When a customer was moved out of a shared organization while still connected, subscriptions they had already opened for tickets of that organization continued to receive updates, such as ticket title, state and newly added public articles, even though regular requests correctly denied access.

The exposure was limited to tickets the customer had already subscribed to before the change, applied only to organizations with shared ticket access, and ended as soon as the connection was re-established. It was read-only. Installations where customers do not change organizations, or that do not use shared organizations, were not affected.

summary: Overview cache could disclose tickets to users without access
description:
The cache used for ticket overviews in the new desktop interface did not take all ticket access rules into account. Users with the same group permissions shared one cache entry, even if they could see different tickets because they were also customers of their own tickets or members of a shared organization.

As a result, an authenticated user could have been shown tickets in an overview that they were not authorized to access. Exposed were the ticket attributes displayed in the overview list, such as number, title, customer and state. The user could not choose which tickets were disclosed.

Affected were installations with users that hold both agent and customer permissions, or with overviews assigned to the Customer role that do not restrict tickets to the current user.

cwes.name: Use of Cache Containing Sensitive Information

summary: Agents could receive ticket notifications shortly after role-based group access was revoked
description:
After an agent lost access to a group through a role change, Zammad could still send that agent ticket notifications for that group for up to 20 seconds. This applied when a role was removed from the agent, when a group was removed from one of the agent's roles, or when such a role was deactivated. Removing a group directly from the agent was not affected.

During this window, the agent could receive online and email notifications for tickets in the group they could no longer access. These notifications could contain the ticket title, the changed ticket attributes, and the article content including inline attachments. The agent could neither trigger such notifications nor choose the ticket; only tickets that were updated by others within the window were exposed.

summary: Agents can read arbitrary ticket articles via online notifications
description:
An authenticated agent could read the content of any ticket article in the system, including internal notes and articles in tickets of groups the agent had no access to. The disclosed data comprised the article body, sender and recipient details, and the core data of the related ticket such as title, state, customer and owner. File attachments themselves remained protected.

The prerequisite was an agent account that had received at least one online notification, which happens in normal use. Once exploited, access persisted even after the agent's group permissions or agent role were revoked, until the account was deactivated.

A similar issue allowed agents to see titles and metadata of unpublished knowledge base answers.

summary: Unauthenticated creation of administrator accounts during a data migration
description:
While a data migration from another helpdesk system was running, the endpoints for creating the first administrator account during system set-up remained publicly accessible. An unauthenticated attacker who could reach the Zammad instance during this time could have created their own administrator account and thereby gained full control over the system, including all migrated tickets, users and configuration data.

Only installations that were being set up via a migration (import) were affected. The exposure lasted for the duration of the migration, and indefinitely if a migration failed and was not completed. Installations set up without a migration, or whose migration had finished successfully, were not affected.

summary: AI-generated ticket field values could disclose protected system settings
description:
When an AI agent that writes AI-generated text into ticket fields was enabled, such as the "Ticket Title Rewriter", a customer could craft the content of a ticket so that the generated value was processed as a template on the server. This could have caused protected system settings, such as the application secret and credentials stored for configured integrations and the AI provider, to be written into a ticket field the customer could read, for example the ticket title.

The attack required an AI provider and such an AI agent to be configured by an administrator, and it depended on the language model following instructions embedded in the ticket content. Installations without AI agents were not affected.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
Improper Neutralization of Special Elements Used in a Template Engine

summary: HTML injection in WhatsApp reaction notification emails
description:
Email notifications about reactions to WhatsApp messages did not escape the reacting contact's display name and reaction before inserting them into the HTML email sent to agents.

Any WhatsApp contact could therefore place HTML markup into Zammad notification emails received by agents, without needing an account or any permission in Zammad. This could have been used to make a trusted notification email show spoofed content, phishing links or forms, or remote images that reveal when and where the email was opened. Script execution in Zammad itself was not possible, and no ticket data was exposed.

Only installations with an active WhatsApp channel were affected, and only agents who receive email notifications for ticket updates. The actual effect depended on how the agent's email client handled HTML content.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation
Improper Neutralization of Script-Related HTML Tags in a Web Page

summary: Local privilege escalation to root in DEB/RPM packages (packager.io)
description:
Zammad packages built with packager.io (DEB and RPM) could have allowed a local attacker who already had code execution as the unprivileged `zammad` service account to escalate to full `root` privileges on the host. Service processes began running as `root` and executed files that were owned and writable by the `zammad` account before dropping to that account, and the installation directory was writable by it. An attacker holding that foothold could have escalated within seconds, because the affected services were restarted automatically whenever they stopped; no administrator interaction was required. Only installations from the DEB and RPM packages were affected — installations from source or the official container images were not. All released packaged versions were affected.

Credit: The Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure Foundation (DIVD)

cwes.name: Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource

summary: Disclosure of user profile data to customer-privileged accounts via the ticket creation form
description:
When the ticket creation form was opened for a particular customer, Zammad returned that account's stored profile data without checking whether the requesting user was allowed to see it. The request was accepted from accounts holding only customer permissions, and the account it referred to could be freely chosen, so a single low-privileged account could have read the profile of every user on the instance, including agents and administrators.

The data returned covered first and last name, email address, telephone and mobile number, VIP status and out-of-office periods, together with the name, domain and VIP status of the account's organization. Passwords, tokens and ticket content were not reachable this way, and nothing could be modified.

On instances where self-registration was enabled, anyone able to create an account was in a position to do this; elsewhere it required an existing customer account.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Sender identity spoofing via headers inside encrypted or signed emails
description:
When the S/MIME or PGP integration was enabled, an unauthenticated remote sender could make an incoming email appear to originate from a different address. By placing a forged sender inside encrypted content, or inside a signed message with an untrusted signature, the resulting ticket or article could be attributed to another existing customer, an agent, or a system address, including that user's account.

Sender authentication performed by the mail infrastructure, such as SPF, DKIM or DMARC, did not prevent this. Agents could be misled into acting on requests that seemingly came from a trusted person. Installations without S/MIME or PGP integration enabled were not affected.

summary: Encrypted or signed incoming email could reintroduce privileged headers past the untrusted-mail filter
description:
When the S/MIME or PGP integration was enabled, Zammad could take internal control headers from the content of encrypted incoming emails, and of certain signed S/MIME emails, although it removes these headers from mail received through untrusted channels. An unauthenticated remote sender could use this to add articles to existing tickets, have them recorded as written by another user, and change ticket attributes such as owner, group, state and customer. By assigning a ticket to a customer account they controlled, an attacker could also gain access to its content and attachments in the customer portal.

Exploitation required an active S/MIME or PGP integration. Neither a trusted certificate nor a valid signature was needed: for encrypted mail, the publicly distributed certificate or key of a Zammad email address was enough.

summary: Stored XSS in desktop autocomplete fields via unescaped option label
description:
Zammad's desktop interface rendered an autocomplete option label as HTML whenever the label did not contain the text the agent had typed. Only labels matching that text were escaped, and a server-side search regularly returns records whose label does not contain it — a user found by email address, shown by name — so unescaped labels reached the browser during ordinary work.

Those labels came from user and organization names, which anyone able to register an account could set. Crafted markup in a name was therefore parsed by the browser and executed in the session of the agent who looked the record up, with that agent's permissions.

The legacy interface and the mobile interface were not affected.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation
Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output

summary: Multi-factor authentication could be bypassed through the email verification flow
description:
Zammad's email verification flow established a fully authenticated session for an existing user account without requiring the second factor configured for that account. Multi-factor authentication was enforced during a normal sign-in, but not on this path.

An account was affected if it had never completed email verification — the default state for accounts created by an administrator, through the API, a directory import, or an incoming email — and had multi-factor authentication configured. Exploitation required possession of the verification email sent to the account's own address; knowing the address was not sufficient, and no password was needed. The resulting session carried the full permissions of the account, up to administrator, and could be used to create a personal access token that outlived it.

Installations relying on multi-factor authentication for agent or administrator accounts are affected most.

summary: Stored XSS in desktop tree select fields via whitespace-only filter
description:
Zammad's new desktop interface rendered option labels in tree select fields as HTML instead of plain text when the dropdown filter contained only whitespace, which happens routinely while typing or deleting a search term. A label containing specially crafted markup was then parsed by the browser instead of being displayed literally.

Tree select labels come from object attribute options, group names and knowledge base category titles. A user with permission to maintain any of these, for example a knowledge base editor or an administrator limited to object management, could have stored such a label. Script embedded in it could have executed in the session of any other agent or administrator who opened the affected field and filtered it, allowing actions and data access with the victim's permissions.

Only the desktop interface was affected; the legacy interface and the mobile interface were not.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation
Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output

summary: Group collection push disclosed full group records to any authenticated session
description:
Zammad pushed complete group records to every connected browser session over the WebSocket collection update, without applying the field scope that limits group data for non-agent users. Any authenticated user, including a customer with no agent permissions, received all attributes of every group in the system whenever a group was created, changed or deleted.

The disclosed data included internal administrative notes, group configuration such as assignment timeouts and shared-draft and signature settings, the list of member user IDs of each group, and groups that were inactive or that the user had no relationship to. No ticket content and no personal contact data were exposed, and the push was read-only, so no group could be altered this way.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Password reset endpoint disclosed whether an account existed via response timing
description:
Zammad's password reset function answered every request identically, so that it would not reveal whether an account exists for the submitted email address or login. The time the request took differed, however, depending on whether an account was found, because further processing was only performed in that case. An unauthenticated user able to reach the login screen could therefore determine whether a given address belonged to an active Zammad account.

Only that fact was exposed. No personal data, ticket content or other account information could be read, and nothing could be modified. The password reset function had to be enabled and outgoing email had to be configured for the difference to be observable. Existing rate limits — three requests per minute per source IP address and per submitted address — restricted how many addresses could be checked. Both the classic and the new interface were affected.

Reported by: Gabriele PARIS from NATO Cyber Security Centre (NCSC)

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Activity stream disclosed content of tickets moved out of an agent's groups
description: Zammad's activity stream returned information about tickets that the requesting agent was no longer allowed to open. Once a ticket had been moved into a group the agent has no access to, or the agent's access to its group had been withdrawn, activity entries recorded earlier remained visible to that agent. Depending on which representation of the activity stream was requested, those entries disclosed the ticket's title, number, current group and customer, and the subject and body of its articles, although the ticket itself was correctly refused. Only agents who previously had access to the affected ticket were able to see this; customers were not affected, and no data could be changed this way.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Group configuration and email address disclosure to authenticated users via getting started endpoint
description:
An API endpoint that supplies start-up information to the web interface required a valid login, but did not check what the account was permitted to see. Any authenticated user, including a customer without agent or administrator permissions, could read the configuration of all active groups — internal group notes, signature and sender-address assignments, and internal ticket handling settings — together with the full list of configured email addresses. Groups the account had no relationship to were included as well.

The exposure was read-only. No ticket content and no personal data of users or customers were affected. Installations that allow customer self-registration, or that keep internal remarks in group notes, are most affected.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Ticket link list disclosed the existence and relation of tickets outside the user's permission scope
description:
The REST endpoint listing an object's links required a session, but never checked whether the requesting user was allowed to see the object they asked about. Any authenticated user, including a customer without agent permissions, could therefore learn that a ticket outside their permission scope existed and was linked to one of their own tickets, and of what link type. As ticket ids are sequential, this could be repeated to find every such link.

No content of the inaccessible ticket was exposed: title, number, customer, group and articles stayed protected, and only links to objects the requester could already read were revealed. Installations that never link tickets across permission boundaries were unaffected, as was the GraphQL API.

summary: Ticket data of no-longer-accessible tickets disclosed to agents via online notification API
description:
Agents who had received an in-app notification about a ticket kept read access to it after losing access — because the ticket moved to a group they cannot see, or their group permissions were narrowed. Opening the ticket was correctly refused, but the notification could still be fetched individually through the API, and its response carried the ticket's title, number, state, priority, escalation data, owner and customer assignment, plus the linked users' names and email addresses.

Only a valid agent account and an existing notification were required, with no action by anyone else. Exposure was limited to tickets the agent still held a notification for, and notifications are retained only for a limited period; other users' notifications were not reachable. Responses carried current data, so later changes were disclosed too. Only installations using group-based access to separate agents from tickets were affected.

cwes.name: Exposure of Private Personal Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Disclosure of names of users from other organizations to customers
description:
Users can be assigned to further organizations in addition to their primary one. Customers are only meant to see the name and active state of their own organization, but due to a missing check on one attribute, a customer reading their own organization also received the list of users assigned to it as secondary members, along with the names of those users.

As a result, a customer could learn the names of users who belong to other organizations. Only names, the active state and avatar information were exposed, no contact details, notes or ticket content, and nothing could be modified this way. Only instances that use secondary organization assignments are affected.

cwes.name: Insertion of Sensitive Information Into Sent Data
Exposure of Private Personal Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Deactivated roles still granted ticket group access in overviews and search
description:
Deactivating a role in Zammad did not revoke the group access it granted. An agent who still held such a deactivated role, and who could still sign in through another active role with agent permissions, retained access to everything scoped by those groups: tickets stayed listed in overviews, search and ticket selection, exposing metadata such as title, number, customer, state and owner, and group-restricted text modules, macros and shared ticket drafts remained available as well.

Opening an affected ticket was correctly refused, so ticket article content stayed protected and no ticket could be changed. Only installations that revoked access by deactivating a role while leaving it assigned to users were affected; administrators who did so should assume the affected agents retained that access throughout.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Deactivated roles still granted knowledge base editor access
description:
Zammad did not check whether a role was still active when resolving the knowledge base access that role granted. A user who still held a role an administrator had set to inactive therefore kept editor access: they could read internal categories and answers that are not published on the public help site, and create, modify and permanently delete them.

The impact was limited to knowledge base content; no ticket data, user records or credentials were exposed. Only installations that deactivated a role carrying knowledge base permissions while it was still assigned to users were affected; administrators who withdrew access that way should review those users' knowledge base activity.

summary: Session identifier disclosed in authenticated configuration response enabled off-host session takeover
description:
Zammad returned the signed-in user's session identifier in an authenticated configuration response, where scripts running in that user's browser were able to read it — which the session cookie's `HttpOnly` flag is meant to prevent. The real-time channel of the classic web interface also accepted such an identifier as proof of identity.

An attacker who had already gained script execution in a user's session, through a separate weakness, could copy the identifier to a machine of their own and act as that user from there for the life of the session, without their password or second factor. This included reading everything the account could see, such as tickets with their internal notes, and creating or changing data in the user's name. The reach scaled with the privileges of the affected account.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
Reliance on Untrusted Inputs in a Security Decision

summary: Inactive sessions remain authorized over ActionCable GraphQL
description:
An account that had been deactivated in Zammad could retain access to ticket data through Zammad's real-time WebSocket connections. The web-based HTTP interface correctly rejected such accounts after deactivation, but the WebSocket connections restored the session's user without applying the same check for whether the account was still active.

As a result, a deactivated agent could continue to read tickets within the scope of their previous group and role assignments, and a deactivated customer could continue to read their own ticket history and shared-organization data, until the underlying session expired or was removed. Because these connections also carry Zammad's live updates, the exposure was not limited to data that already existed at the point of deactivation: ticket changes and notifications occurring afterwards could continue to reach the affected account. The issue required an existing, retained session for an account that was later deactivated; it did not allow a new account, or an attacker without a valid session, to gain access.

Administrators who deactivated accounts while running an affected version should treat any sessions still stored for those accounts as potentially usable and remove them in addition to upgrading. Installations in which no account was ever deactivated were not exposed.

summary: Remote code execution via template sanitizer bypass in automation configuration
description:
A user allowed to configure automations in Zammad — such as triggers, scheduled jobs, ticket macros or AI agents — could execute arbitrary commands on the server hosting Zammad. A specially crafted value in an automation's configuration bypassed the escaping Zammad applied to such text, and the resulting code ran with the privileges of the Zammad application process. No interaction from another user was required.

This could have been used to read or modify any data reachable by that process, including the ticket and customer database and any credentials available to it. On a default installation the required permission is held only by full administrators, who already have supported ways of running code on the server, so the practical gain there was limited; it became a genuine privilege escalation where a scoped or delegated role, or a hosted deployment, granted automation configuration without full administrative access. Installations with AI agents configured were exposed on an additional path, because values returned by the configured AI provider were processed in the same way.

cwes.name: Improper Control of Generation of Code
Improper Neutralization of Special Elements Used in a Template Engine

summary: Unfiltered sign-up and ticket update fields allow cross-organization ticket disclosure and takeover
description:
Zammad's public sign-up form accepted account fields that it should have ignored. An attacker without any account could use this to register on an email address they did not own, have that account treated as already email-confirmed, and add it to any organization in the system.

Because members of an organization can see each other's tickets by default, such an account could then read and reply to tickets of other customers of those organizations. A second issue allowed any customer account to change fields of another customer's ticket in the same organization — including which customer the ticket belongs to — which could take a ticket away from the person who opened it.

cwes.name: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes

summary: Stored XSS in ticket zoom via attacker-controlled article preferences
description:
A customer was able to store content of their own choosing in the internal metadata of a ticket article they created. When an agent later opened that ticket, parts of this metadata were displayed without being neutralized for safe rendering, so the stored content was interpreted as active content in the agent's browser session.

As a result, a user with only standard customer permissions was able to cause code to run in the session of any agent who opened the affected ticket, without any special configuration or elevated privileges. Because the code ran with the agent's session, its impact extended to whatever that agent could reach, including tickets in other groups and internal notes.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation
Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes

summary: Arbitrary configuration disclosure via recent view endpoint
description:
Any authenticated user, including the lowest-privileged customer role, could read the name and stored value of arbitrary application configuration settings. Because the configuration also holds deployment secrets, this included credentials a non-administrative user would otherwise never reach, such as the Elasticsearch endpoint password and the credentials of configured import sources.

Affected were all settings neither marked as protected nor restricted to a specific permission — roughly a quarter of all settings on a default installation, including the credential-bearing ones. Sensitive values existed only where the corresponding feature was configured. Access was read-only and limited to configuration data.

Upgrading does not undo an exposure that already happened. Administrators should rotate the affected credentials after upgrading.

Reported by: Gabriele PARIS from NATO Cyber Security Centre (NCSC)

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Second-order SQL injection in ticket overview sorting
description:
Zammad's ticket overview handling contained a second-order SQL injection flaw. A user permitted to create or modify ticket overviews could store a crafted value in an overview's sort-order configuration. That value was not restricted to the expected sort keywords, and when tickets for the overview were later retrieved through the API, it was incorporated into the underlying database query without being safely escaped for that context. Triggering it required no action by any other user.

An attacker able to reach this could have read arbitrary data from the Zammad database — including other users' password hashes, ticket content and configuration data — regardless of what their own role was meant to grant them access to. The further reachable impact depended on the privileges of the database account the installation runs Zammad with. Installations using the packaged (Linux) setup, where Zammad runs with a restricted non-superuser database role, were limited to that read impact; where the database role held elevated privileges, the same access could have been extended to reading and writing files on the database host and, from there, to executing arbitrary code with the privileges of the database server process.

Reported by: Gabriele PARIS from NATO Cyber Security Centre (NCSC)

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command
Improper Control of Generation of Code

summary: Unscoped GraphQL template query and subscription bypass TemplatePolicy scope
description:
Ticket templates were not restricted to the users allowed to see them. Agents were able to see templates that had been deactivated, and customers were able to receive the contents of all templates — including deactivated ones — whenever any template was created, changed or deleted.

The disclosed information covered the name of each template and the values it fills in, such as prepared ticket titles, message texts, and the customer, group, owner or tag settings stored in it. Access was limited to reading; it was not possible to change templates, tickets or any other data this way. How sensitive the disclosed information was depended on what each installation had stored in its templates.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Stored HTML injection in Knowledge Base video widget rendered inside Zammad enables forced session switching
description:
A user with Knowledge Base editing rights for a category can embed a video widget in an answer with a specially crafted value. When that answer is opened in Zammad's knowledge base view, the value is inserted into the page's HTML without being escaped for the context it appears in, allowing it to break out and inject additional HTML into the page. The answer does not need to be published for this to happen.

When another user who has permission to switch between user sessions opens the affected answer, the injected HTML causes their browser to silently send a request to Zammad's session-switching endpoint using their own active credentials. This results in switching their session to an account chosen by the person who wrote the Knowledge Base answer. No action is required from the viewer beyond opening the answer.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation

summary: Missing authorization on ticket articles can expose article content to unauthorized users
description: A missing authorization check in the ticket-article creation endpoint allows any authenticated customer to read the content of arbitrary ticket articles, including internal agent notes and articles belonging to other organizations, that they are not permitted to view. This constitutes a confidentiality break of Zammad's core ticketing data, requiring no elevated privileges and no user interaction.

summary: Channel administration APIs return stored channel credentials in clear text
description:
Zammad stores the access data of the configured channels, such as Facebook page access tokens, the Telegram bot token, the SMS gateway token and the passwords or OAuth tokens of email accounts. Whenever a channel configuration is sent to the browser, these values are supposed to be replaced by a masked placeholder, so that stored access data cannot be read back once it has been saved. For several channels this masking did not take effect.

As a result, an administrator holding the permission for one of the affected channels could obtain the stored access data in clear text through the channel administration APIs, and use it to access the connected external service directly, outside of Zammad. Affected are the Facebook, Telegram, SMS and email channels, including the Google and Microsoft 365 variants.

Only instances that have such a channel configured are affected, and only administrators who already hold the administration permission for that channel type could read the access data.

cwes.name: Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output
Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Forward quote header discloses agent email addresses
description:
When an agent forwarded an existing message from a ticket, the quoted message header that Zammad generated could contain the personal email address of the agent who wrote the original message, instead of the shared email address of the group.

As a result, that agent's personal address could be sent to the external recipient of the forwarded message. Because the forwarded message is stored as a publicly visible article, the address was also readable by the customer of the ticket, even though customers are otherwise never given the email addresses of agents.

Only instances whose sender format for outgoing email is configured to show the agent name alone are affected. Instances using the default sender format are not affected.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
Exposure of Private Personal Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Clipboard HTML injection via unescaped user and organization display name
description:
The desktop view offers a button to copy a user's or an organization's name together with a link to their profile. The copied content was assembled without properly escaping the name, so a name that contains markup was copied as markup rather than as plain text.

An attacker could use this by choosing a crafted name — for example by sending an email into the helpdesk with a specially prepared sender name, which does not require an account. If an agent then copies that name and pastes it into a formatted text field, such as a reply to a customer, the pasted content can contain a link or other elements chosen by the attacker instead of the intended profile link. This can be used to make a message written by an agent point recipients at an attacker-controlled destination.

cwes.name: Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output

summary: Customer-visible ticket update responses leak unredacted user and organization data
description:
Ticket update responses could include unredacted personal data that should have been hidden from the requesting user.

When a customer updated one of their own tickets and requested a detailed response, the reply could contain unfiltered details about the agents involved in that ticket - such as private phone numbers, postal address, department and internal notes - as well as internal information about their organization, including internal notes and the VIP flag. The same data is correctly hidden when simply viewing the ticket; only the update responses were affected.

Customers could therefore obtain personal information about support staff and internal administrative notes that are meant for internal use only.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
Exposure of Private Personal Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Knowledge base reordering, publishing and administration possible without the required permission
description:
Agents with read-only knowledge base access were able to change the order of knowledge base categories and answers, and to change the publication state of answers. Both are intended to be restricted to knowledge base editors, but the permission checks accepted any level of knowledge base access. Because agents receive read access by default, any agent could publish answers to the public help site, archive or un-archive them, and set the publication dates. Answers meant to stay internal could therefore be made available to anonymous visitors, and published answers could be removed from the site.

Separately, agents with knowledge base editor access were able to create, change and delete knowledge bases themselves, although this is reserved for knowledge base administrators. An editor could change the public address and the appearance of a knowledge base, take it offline, or delete it together with all of its categories and answers.

summary: Cross-tenant attachment disclosure via inline images in notification emails
description:
Zammad could attach files belonging to unrelated tickets or knowledge base articles to outgoing notification emails.

If a trigger or scheduler is configured to send a notification email that quotes the incoming message in HTML, anyone able to send an email to the system could craft a message that causes an arbitrary stored file from the instance to be included as an attachment in the reply they receive. No account or login is required.

As a result, attachments from other customers' tickets or from internal knowledge base articles could be disclosed to an outside party.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Disclosure of group-restricted text modules to unauthorized agents
description:
Text modules (canned responses) can be limited to specific groups, or deactivated so they are no longer offered. Due to a missing permission check, any logged-in agent was able to retrieve a single text module directly and see its full content, even if it belonged to a group they have no access to.

As a result, internal reply templates could become visible to agents who were not meant to see
them. No ticket or customer data was affected, and the text modules could not be changed this way.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Improper access control allows agents to read and modify other users' overview ordering preferences
description:
Zammad did not check record ownership when handling requests to the personal overview ordering endpoints.

Because of this, any logged-in agent was able to read, change or delete the overview ordering preferences of any other user, and to create such preferences on another user's behalf.

The impact is limited to the order and sorting in which ticket overviews are presented to the affected users; no ticket content or other personal data was exposed through this.

summary: Disclosure of external data source credentials to non-admin users via object attribute metadata
description:
Object attributes that look up their values from an external data source store the access data for that external system (user name, password or access token, and the request URL) as part of their configuration. This configuration was sent to every logged-in user, including agents and customers, instead of being kept on the server and restricted to administrators.

As a result, any logged-in user of an affected instance could read the stored access data and use it to access the connected external system directly, outside of Zammad. Only instances that have configured an external data source attribute with access data are affected.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Arbitrary object disclosure via Core Workflow perform endpoint
description:
A logged-in user with only agent or customer permissions could ask Zammad for the details of almost any single record in the system - for example configuration settings, other users' unsaved drafts, or their device and login information - simply by naming the record in a request. Zammad returned that data without checking whether the user was allowed to see it.

Among the data that could be read were confidential configuration values such as the application secret, the monitoring access token, and third-party login credentials. Ticket data remained protected, and stored passwords were not exposed.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: AI error messages can be turned into clickable links due to incorrect escaping order
description:
When a Zammad AI feature (writing assistant or ticket summary) fails, the resulting error message is shown to the agent in the interface. Because of a flaw in how that message is escaped before display, an error message containing link-style text could be rendered as an actual clickable link in the agent's browser instead of being shown as harmless plain text. In unfavorable conditions this could be used to present misleading links or, depending on the browser and its security settings, inject unwanted content into the page.

Exploitation requires an authenticated agent with AI features enabled and depends on an attacker being able to influence the AI error text, so real-world impact is limited.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation
Improper Neutralization of Script in Attributes in a Web Page
Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output

summary: Stored XSS in ticket article rendering in the new Vue-based interface
description:
Under certain conditions, the new Vue-based interface could render ticket article content without applying the expected output encoding. This could be triggered by an authenticated user and affect other users viewing the ticket.

The default Content Security Policy limits the real-world impact. The classic REST/CoffeeScript interface is not affected.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation
Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output

summary: SSRF protection bypass via DNS rebinding in hostname safety check
description: Zammad validates a URL's resolved IP before fetching it, to prevent the server from being tricked into reaching internal-only addresses (SSRF) such as loopback or cloud-metadata endpoints. The validation and the actual request resolve the hostname separately, without pinning the checked IP. An attacker controlling DNS for a domain can return a safe address during validation and an internal one for the request, bypassing the protection. This affects all features using the check - calendar (iCal) subscriptions, webhooks, avatar fetching, and external data sources. Exploitation requires an admin to configure the attacker-supplied URL and depends on a DNS-timing race, but needs no attacker privileges on the instance.

cwes.name: Reliance on Reverse DNS Resolution for a Security-Critical Action

summary: S/MIME signature verification allows forged sender impersonation
description:
When Zammad checks the digital signature on an incoming S/MIME-signed email, it does not verify that the signing certificate is genuinely trusted - it only checks whether a certificate with a matching name is already stored in the system.

An attacker can create their own certificate using the name of a real, previously trusted sender and use it to send a forged email. 

Zammad will display that email with the same "validly signed" indicator as a genuine message from the real sender, even though the attacker never had access to that sender's actual certificate or private key.

summary: Stored HTML injection in Knowledge Base video widget enables forced session switching via unescaped iframe attribute
description:
A user with Knowledge Base editing rights for a category can embed a video widget in a published answer with a specially crafted value. When the answer is rendered, that value is inserted into the page's HTML without being escaped for its attribute context, allowing it to break out and inject additional HTML into the page.

When another user who has permission to switch between user sessions views the affected answer, the injected HTML causes their browser to silently send a request to Zammad's session-switching endpoint using their own active credentials. This results in switching their session to an account chosen by the person who wrote the Knowledge Base answer. No action is required from the viewer beyond opening the published answer.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation

summary: Missing Authorization in TagsController#list Allows Cross-Object Tag Enumeration
description: Any authenticated user can call the REST endpoint for getting a tag list and receive the tag names for the given ticket, regardless of whether they have access to that ticket. Tags are an internal categorization feature and may contain sensitive labels. Ticket IDs are sequential integers, making bulk enumeration straightforward.

summary: IDOR in External Data Source rendering exposes ticket, user, group, and organization data
description:
Zammad's External Data Source feature, used to look up records from an external system, did not properly verify whether a user was allowed to see a specific ticket, user, group, or organization before including its details in a request to that external system.

An authenticated user, including one with only basic customer access, could exploit this by referencing another record's ID, and thereby view details of tickets, customer accounts, teams, or organizations that did not belong to them.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: AI Agent template sanitizer bypass leads to remote code execution
description: A security filter that protects Zammad's AI Agent configuration can be bypassed by entering specially crafted text into one of an AI Agent's fields. An administrator with permission to create or edit AI Agents could exploit this to run arbitrary commands on the server that hosts Zammad - potentially reading, modifying, or destroying all data stored on that server. No interaction from other users is needed; the malicious code runs automatically the next time the affected AI Agent processes a ticket.

cwes.name: Improper Control of Generation of Code
Improper Neutralization of Special Elements Used in a Template Engine

summary: Missing rate limiting allows password brute-forcing during two-factor login
description: The two-factor login step let an attacker try unlimited password guesses for any account without triggering Zammad's normal lockout or rate limiting. The response also revealed whether a guess was correct, even before two-factor authentication was checked. This made it possible to brute-force weak or reused passwords.

cwes.name: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts

summary: Pending upload deletion bypass via legacy attachment endpoint
description: The legacy `destroy_form` action on AttachmentsController deletes UploadCache Store records based solely on a user-supplied `form_id` without verifying that the requesting user owns those records. An authenticated attacker who learns another user's pending-upload UUID can silently remove temporary file uploads before the victim submits their ticket or article.

summary: Account takeover via unverified email matching during SSO auto-link
description:
When the "Automatic account link on initial logon" setting is enabled, Zammad binds an incoming third-party (SSO) identity to an existing local account by matching the email address the identity provider reports, without verifying that the provider actually confirmed ownership of that email. An attacker who controls any identity at a configured provider - including, by default, any Azure AD tenant via Zammad's multi-tenant Microsoft 365 `/common` app registration - can set that identity's email to a victim's address, authenticate, and be logged in as the victim. This bypasses the victim's local password entirely and affects any existing account, including agents and administrators.

Zammad will honor the `xms_edov` ID token claim when email verification is required in the Microsoft 365 setting, treating a missing claim as unverified.

summary: Authenticated agents can read AI summary error messages from inaccessible tickets
description: An authenticated user with agent permissions can supply an arbitrary AI analytics run identifier to the ticket summarize endpoint and receive the AI provider error message stored for that run, even if the run belongs to a ticket the agent is not authorized to access. The disclosure is limited to the provider error string; ticket content is not exposed.

summary: Channel admins can read unauthorized attachments via signature rich-text body
description:
When creating or updating an email signature, Zammad processes inline images referenced in the signature body. If a signature body contains an HTML `img` tag pointing to any existing attachment, the system copies that attachment into a new signature-owned record - without checking whether the user has permission to access the original attachment.

The newly created copy is then downloadable by the same channel-admin user, because attachment access is determined by the copy's owner (the signature), not the original object (e.g., a ticket or knowledge-base article). This allows a user with any of the `admin.channel_email`, `admin.channel_google`, `admin.channel_microsoft365`, or `admin.channel_microsoft_graph` permissions to read attachments they would otherwise be denied access to, such as ticket attachments belonging to groups they are not a member of.

summary: Microsoft Graph error logs expose partially masked OAuth access tokens
description:
When a Microsoft Graph request fails, Zammad logs the error including the authentication token used to access the mailbox.

The system attempts to hide this token in the log, but the masking is incomplete: for the token format Microsoft uses (JWT), only the first part is hidden, while the remaining parts remain readable in plain text.
